Kennedy Space Center LC-39B, planned for early 2028. Artemis IV is planned as the first crewed lunar landing since Apollo 17 (1972) and the first crewed landing near the south pole. SLS Block 1 flies for the last time with the ICPS upper stage, carrying Orion and four crew.
The ICPS burn sends Orion and its crew on a 4-day coast to Near-Rectilinear Halo Orbit, where the commercial lander — Starship HLS or Blue Moon, not yet chosen — waits.

Orion captures into Near-Rectilinear Halo Orbit — an elongated lunar orbit with a 3,000 km perilune and a 70,000 km apolune, much cheaper to reach than Apollo's circular low lunar orbit (~0.45 km/s against Apollo's 0.89 km/s). The crew docks with the waiting lander.
Lander powered descent — lunar south pole

Two crew descend in the lander while two remain in Orion. The target is the south polar region, where NASA has named nine candidate landing regions. A surface stay of about a week is planned — more than twice Apollo's longest, about 3 days on Apollo 17.
The lander lifts off and carries the two surface crew back to NRHO, where they transfer to Orion.
Orion leaves NRHO on its return trajectory, about ten days after arriving.
Planned for early 2028. Orion re-enters Earth's atmosphere at lunar-return velocity (~11 km/s) and splashes down in the Pacific.
First crewed lunar landing since Apollo 17 (1972)

Since NASA's February 2026 change of plan, Artemis IV is the mission that returns people to the lunar surface — the first crewed landing since Apollo 17 in 1972, and the first crewed landing near the south pole. SLS, on its last flight with the interim upper stage, launches Orion with four crew towards the Moon. In lunar orbit they meet a commercial lander — SpaceX's Starship or Blue Origin's Blue Moon, chosen after the Artemis III docking tests — and two astronauts descend to the south polar region for about a week of surface work, while two remain aboard Orion. The south pole is the target because its permanently shadowed craters hold water ice, which future missions may turn into drinking water, oxygen and rocket propellant. NASA has identified nine candidate landing regions. Planned for early 2028; the crew has not yet been named.
Orion launches from KSC LC-39B with crew of 4.
Orion arrives in a high lunar orbit and meets the waiting lander.
2 crew transfer to the lander; powered descent to the lunar south pole.
The lander returns to lunar orbit after about a week of surface operations.
Orion splashes down in the Pacific Ocean.
